newsitem.title: HONG KONG: WEEK AHEAD - Further weakness seen in Asian stocks.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD - Further weakness seen in Asian stocks.

text.p: Asian stocks are set for more disappointment in the week ahead, with Hong Kong once again offering the only upward momentum in a region under pressure from weak investor sentiment.
Recent currency turmoil and falling growth prospects have highlighted Asia's declining competitiveness in the battle for emerging market fund investment, dealers said.
"It's very quiet," one head trader said. "There's better value elsewhere. We even had a Latin American person out here explaining why they offered better value. It was convincing."
A technical bounce is considered possible in the Philippines, while the tense Indonesian election campaign is expected to put a damper on stocks in Jakarta.
Thailand is considered unlikely to make any gains, but the outlook is more mixed in Malaysia and Singapore.

TOKYO - Japanese stocks are likely to consolidate recent gains in the coming week and may even push further beyond the 20,000-point level but the currency turbulence that knocked the wind out of export issues in the past week needed to be watched carefully, brokers said.
"There is a fair amount of volatility in the currency market which means that time will be needed for calm to return," said Masaaki Higashida, Nomura Securities strategist.
The Nikkei average started the previous week at a new high for the year of 20,489.75 but was buffeted soon after by the yen's surge past 112 to the dollar during the week.
On Friday, the Nikkei average rose 131.61 points or 0.66 percent, to end 2.35 percent higher on the week at 20,009.
HONG KONG - Hong Kong stocks are set to move ahead, boosted by positive sentiment surrounding the territory's most successful IPO ever and bargain-hunting on any weakness, analysts said.
Red chips are expected to be the focus with China-backed Beijing Enterprises Holdings Ltd's market debut on Thursday.
Blue chips are also expected to be well supported by rotational buying, analysts said.
The Hang Seng Index continued to hit record highs last week, ending it with a record close of 14,331.68 on Friday. The index gained 269.31 points, or 1.92 percent, over the week.
BANGKOK - The Thai stock market is expected to fall in the week ahead unless Thai banks cut interest rates.
The announcement on Friday of the collapse of the proposed merger between Thai Danu Bank Plc and Finance One Plc had cast a negative tone over the battered market, brokers said.
The SET index rose 3.6 percent to 581.13 for the week.
JAKARTA - Jakarta stocks are likely to be mixed in the coming week on political fears ahead of the May 29 general election, although the official campaign finished on Friday, brokers said.
Brokers and analysts said the market sentiment was likely to remain weak after violence hit Jakarta during the last round of campaigning, brokers said.
Brokers said expected announcements of some first quarter results and corporate plans of several companies could boost market sentiment.
On Friday, the Jakarta composite index closed at 658.52 points, against the previous week's close of 657.07 points.
KUALA LUMPUR - Retail and local institutional investors are expected to dominate activity with foreign investors steering clear.
On Friday, the Composite Index of 100 large-capitalised stocks rose 7.17 points or 0.67 percent to 1,078.20, a week-on-week gain of 36.29 points or 3.48 percent.
MANILA - Philippine shares are seen moving in a narrow range with a downward bias ahead of the eagerly-awaited release of first quarter GNP figures, traders said.
"We've had all the bad news out last week and we saw three days of successive gains. We will likely see some profit-taking soon," said Spencer Yap, analyst at BPI Securities.
UBS Securities analyst Ivy Cayayan said volumes will be thin as foreigners are still waiting on the sidelines.
On Friday, the main index rose 11.51 points to close at 2,598.20. Week-on-week, the index gained 0.86 percent.
SEOUL - Seoul stocks are expected to move in a boxed range between 715 and 750 points in the week ahead, but any fresh news on the Japanese yen would have an impact, brokers said.
They cited expected interest rate falls in early June and rising customer deposits as positive factors, while rumours of corporate financial troubles remain worrisome.
"Lingering fears over rumours of corporate financial troubles will continue to drag the market for the time being," said Park Man-soon, an analyst at Daishin Securities.
The composite index ended at 725.17 on Saturday, up 2.7 percent or 18.92 points from the previous Saturday's 706.25.
SINGAPORE - Dealers in Singapore said the market would likely drift sideways in the week ahead due to recent poor institutional demand and lack of buying incentives.

"People are adopting a wait-and-see attitude. Most activity will probably be in secondliners," a dealer with a local brokerage said, noting a drop in foreign fund confidence for the Asian region as a whole.
Last Friday, the Straits Times Index closed at 2,055.36, down 6.35 points.

SYDNEY - Australian stocks raced on Friday to their third successive record close as interest rate sensitive sectors like banking, insurance and retail celebrated a surprise cut in official interest rates.
"The reality is, the bears have done their selling and now there's no real incentive to do any more selling," BNP Equities head of sales John Bowie Wilson.
Brokers said the cut in the official cash rate to 5.5 percent to 6.0 percent released an already bullish market from its previous shackles around 2,550 on the All Ordinaries index.
The index closed up 16 points at 2,563.9 on Friday.
TAIPEI - Taiwan share prices are expected to consolidate in the absence of any market-moving factors, following a technical rebound in the past week.
After an initial fall in the week, the index, which dropped to 7996.75 points on Tuesday, slowly recovered following moderate technical rebounds later, brokers said.
"Major sectors, like electronics, steels and plastics, should see some gains next week, but selling sprees are also expected on profit-taking," analyst Oliver Fang of National Securities said.
On Saturday, the benchmark stock index finished 34.32 points or 0.42 percent higher to 8,178.70, down 0.46 percent from 8,141.12 points a week earlier.
A trading range of 7,900-8,300 is seen for next week.
WELLINGTON - The New Zealand share market ended the week 11.15 points lower than last Friday's close, but brokers noted that offshore interest in New Zealand stocks appeared to be returning.
Volumes in the past couple of days have picked up significantly, and a delayed positive response to Australia's 0.5 percent rate cut on Friday was possible next week.
SBC Warburg broker Campbell Stuart said New Zealand equities represented reasonable value at present.
DHAKA - Dhaka stocks' long rally last week ended with a bout of profit-taking before the market closed for the Moslem Friday weekend, brokers said.
Brokers said a market correction was overdue, and said strong market sentiment was likely to move up steadily after an anticipated brief correction.
The Dhaka Stock Exchange benchmark index gained 43.26 points at 1,187.84 in the week to Thursday.
